git add -A && git status --short && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Measure freshness by version, and dispose of a stranded update PR

Two defects the fleet-wide migration surfaced (#786, #787).

FRESHNESS BY VERSION. The update flows stamp `engineVersion`/`packVersions`
and deliberately never write `ref` or `updated` — a no-op cycle must produce
no PR, and a date stamped every night is the churn the versioned scheme
removed. But fleet-freshness measured liveness by the AGE OF THE STAMPED REF,
which on a flipped member is frozen by design. With one canary that was a
curiosity; with the whole fleet migrated it would report every healthy member
as drifting the moment canon moved past the commit baselining last wrote.

The sweep now asks the question the member's own mechanism can answer:
baselining keeps the date measure unchanged, and `updates` compares installed
versions against what canon publishes. That is exact rather than estimated, so
a drift issue names the missing version instead of a number of days, and
`staleDays` is correctly documented as governing only the date half. A
version-measured member never consults the ref at all — neither the compare
call nor the `ref-not-on-trunk` verdict derived from it, both of which would
be answering a question that no longer means anything.

Canon's side is read from canon over the API (never imported — the enforcer's
mount is a different commit, and what canon publishes NOW is the question),
cached so the fleet's shared packs cost one read each per sweep.

DISPOSAL. The update runner logged "leaving it open for the next run to
dispose of" and no code anywhere could keep that promise: the quiet-cycle
early return fires before anything looks at open PRs, so the only cycle that
could dispose of a stranded PR was one with its own work to deliver — and
that cycle opened a competing PR instead. Observed on TLDR #246 and
CrosswordChat #177, both superseded by a duplicate and closed by hand.

Disposal moves out of baselining's worker into the shared landing module,
where the precedence it reuses already lives, and the runner calls it BEFORE
the converge — the ordering is the fix, since disposal after the converge is
unreachable on exactly the quiet cycle that should perform it. It reports
which of three disposals happened, because `merged` means main moved past
this job's checkout and converging on that stale tree would re-deliver a diff
that just landed.
EOF

### README.md
22:  owning pack per skill). No pack is active undeclared — the baseline included; activation is
64:`engine/migrations/` holds the **baseline migrations** mechanism — declared path relocations, one record per canon rename (a renamed or relocated artifact consumers hold their own copy of) that supplies the read-side resolver and the write-side rename. Each record lives under the flow that owns it: an engine change beside the mechanism, a pack's own under `packs/<pack>/migrations/`. 1	// Land a task's delivered pull request under the REPO's delivery settings — the
2	// single home for the auto-merge nuances every PR-delivering task shares. These
3	// helpers were built inside the baselining worker (#455/#565/#649/#677/#690);
4	// they live here because the other `merged-pr` tasks hit the identical failure
5	// shapes (an arm rejected "clean status" on an ungated base stranding a green PR
6	// forever), and two copies of this precedence is exactly the drift the corpus
7	// forbids.
8	//
9	// The contract that keeps tasks simple: a task declares only its outcome CEILING
10	// (`expected_outcome: 'merged-pr'` — it MAY land a PR). Whether the PR actually
11	// lands unreviewed is the MEMBER REPO's call — `maintenance.delivery` in
12	// `.claudinite-checks.json`, where `review` degrades every merged-pr task to
13	// open-pr (member config wins, per-project-scheduling DESIGN §1). Tasks stay
14	// unaware of that setting by construction: they hand their PR to landDelivery()
15	// (directly, or through deliver-generated.mjs) and the repo-shape nuances stay
16	// here:

18	//   - `review` member          → the PR is opened and LEFT — never armed, never merged.
19	//   - no pull_request CI at all → MERGE directly. GitHub's auto-merge is a queue
20	//     for checks; with nothing to queue behind, the arm is rejected ("Pull
21	//     request is in clean status") every time, and while that rejection was

68	// `pr` → review are the permanent legacy aliases (the maintenance-lane tolerance);
69	// anything else is invalid (null) and fails the run rather than guessing.
70	export function normalizeDelivery(raw) {

80	// `maintenance.delivery` is always EXPLICIT — but a key that is simply absent is
81	// DRIFT, not an error. A repo adopted before the key existed, or one whose key

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Phase 5: retire baselining

The last phase of #768. Baselining and the update flows have both existed
since Phase 4 so the fleet could cross over one repo at a time; every member
now declares `maintenance.mechanism: "updates"`, so the older mechanism has
nothing left to serve.

REMOVED. `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/` and its escalation codes; the
`migrations/apply.mjs` and `migrations/registry.mjs` compatibility entry
points (#769) and the empty `migrations/` tree with them.

Those shims existed because a member invoked the applier BY PATH out of a
fresh canon clone, using its own vendored worker — as new as its last
converge, never as new as canon. Deleting them earlier would have failed the
apply step of the very converge that would have delivered the newer worker.
That deadlock is gone with the worker that had it.

THE `agentic:` FIELD IS REJECTED, NOT IGNORED. Nothing reads it: the engine
flow never had an agentic lane (DESIGN §5), and the pack flow's apply stage
decides from the version plan — a fact about what the update did, not a flag
a record carries. An ignored field on a record written in good faith is work
that silently never happens, which is the correctness risk the note existed
to close (#405), so `loadMigrations` fails on one and says where the work
goes now. The last record carrying a note (sheepdog's `fleet-baseline-task`)
is drained — the orphaned workflow it removed is gone from the enforcer.

THE DEFAULT MECHANISM MOVES TO `updates`, by the same rule that once pointed
it at baselining: a default may only point at what is already true. The
retired value still PARSES — a mount predating the flip, or a restored
backup, can still say it, and reading that as anything else would hand the
repo to a mechanism its owner never chose — but the update runner now refuses
such a repo loudly and non-zero instead of standing down, because standing
down quietly leaves a repo unmaintained with a green run to show for it.

The sheepdog fleet lever now forces `update`. A lever naming a task nothing
runs still reports a clean dispatch, and that sweep counts dispatches rather
than outcomes (Sheepdog#172), so the wrong id there would have been invisible.

VOCABULARY. Swept where the word named the LIVE mechanism — instructions,
check remedies, user-facing docs, the scheduler stub's own
`FORCE_TASKS=baselining` example. Deliberately NOT swept in two places: dated
migration records and design docs, which describe a mechanism that really
existed and are history rather than instructions; and the unrelated sense of
"baseline" (the baseline pack, baseline skills, baseline migrations), which
a mechanical rename would have corrupted.

The `fleet-baseline` task keeps its name for now — renaming a pack task is
the fleet-wide update lever's own work, not this change's.

# The LIVE CANARY (#593 phase 3) — the required final step of any core change.
#
# The fixture rehearsal (packs-tests/rehearsal/) is the fast gate: hermetic,
# seconds, on every PR. It has one honest weakness — a fixture only tests what
# someone remembered to model. This is the other half: a REAL repo, really
# adopting Claudinite, really running its own scheduler, converged against this
# canon ref and asked whether it still works.
#
# WHY IT IS A SEPARATE WORKFLOW. It takes minutes, needs a cross-repo token, and
# mutates another repository's working tree. A gate with those properties cannot
# run on every push without becoming something people route around. So: manual
# dispatch, plus automatic on merge to main — the post-merge smoke test, which
# the owner's own framing settles as "still much much better than not knowing".
#
# WHERE THE CANARY IS NAMED. In `.claudinite-checks.json`, on the `local/claudinite`
# pack entry's `config.canaryRepo` — the same tracked pack-entry config mechanism
# the sheepdog pack uses for its fleet scope. NOT a GitHub repository variable: the
# binding between this canon and its canary is a fact about the project, and a
# repository variable is invisible in the tree, absent from every diff, and cannot
# be reviewed alongside the workflow that acts on it. A reader of this repo should
# be able to see which repo CI is about to rewrite.
#
# WHY A DEDICATED REPO, NOT A REAL PROJECT. A rehearsal rewrites the mount and
# can leave a failed converge behind. Pointing that at EdFringeNow means a bad
# canon commit leaves a real project dirty at the exact moment attention is
# elsewhere. The canary is disposable by construction; that is its whole value.
#
# WHAT PROTECTS THE CANARY ITSELF: the worker's rehearsal mode
# (CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF) converges, reports, and then RESTORES the working tree —
# no commit, no branch, no PR, and above all no stamp. Stamping a branch head
# would leave the canary `ref-not-on-trunk`, which vendoring's #328 anti-rewind
# guard then refuses to converge over: a rehearsal that wedges its own canary.
name: Canary rehearsal

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      ref:
        description: "Canon ref to rehearse (blank = this workflow's own ref)"
        required: false
        type: string
  push:
    branches: [main]
    # Only the surfaces a consumer actually vendors. A README or a doc change
    # cannot break a member, and spending minutes proving that teaches everyone

content.content:
# cannot break a member, and spending minutes proving that teaches everyone
    # to ignore the result.
    paths:
      - 'engine/**'
      - 'packs/**'
      - 'vendoring/**'

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  # One canary at a time: two rehearsals converging the same repo would race on
  # its working tree and report each other's damage.
  group: canary-rehearsal
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  rehearse:
    name: Rehearse against the canary repo
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - name: Check out the canon (for the declaration)
        uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - name: Resolve the canary repo from the declaration
        id: cfg
        run: |
          CANARY=$(node -e '
            const c = require("./.claudinite-checks.json");
            const e = (c.packs || []).find((p) => p && p.id === "local/claudinite");
            process.stdout.write(e?.config?.canaryRepo ?? "");
          ')
          if [ -z "$CANARY" ]; then
            echo "::warning::No canary declared — skipping the live canary."
            echo "Add config.canaryRepo to the local/claudinite pack entry in"
            echo ".claudinite-checks.json, naming a disposable repo that has adopted"
            echo "Claudinite. Until then the fixture rehearsal is the only consumer gate."
            echo "skip=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "Canary: $CANARY (from .claudinite-checks.json)"
            echo "skip=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "repo=$CANARY" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi

      - name: Check out the canary
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          repository: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.repo }}
          token: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          path: canary

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        with:
          node-version: '24'

      # The canary runs ITS OWN vendored worker, not this checkout's — that is
      # the copy a member would run, and testing anything else would be testing
      # a code path no consumer ever executes. The worker then fetches THIS ref
      # and converges the canary against it.
      - name: Rehearse
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        env:
          CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF: ${{ inputs.ref || github.ref_name }}
          CLAUDINITE_REPO_ROOT: ${{ github.workspace }}/canary
          CLAUDINITE_REPO: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.repo }}
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        working-directory: canary/.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining
        run: node worker.mjs

      - name: What a failure means
        if: failure()
        run: |
          echo "::error::The canary repo could not be converged against this canon ref."

python3 - <<'PY'
p='.github/workflows/canary-rehearsal.yml'
s=open(p,encoding='utf8').read()
old = """      # The canary runs ITS OWN vendored worker, not this checkout's — that is
      # the copy a member would run, and testing anything else would be testing
      # a code path no consumer ever executes. The worker then fetches THIS ref
      # and converges the canary against it.
      - name: Rehearse
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        env:
          CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF: ${{ inputs.ref || github.ref_name }}
          CLAUDINITE_REPO_ROOT: ${{ github.workspace }}/canary
          CLAUDINITE_REPO: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.repo }}
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        working-directory: canary/.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining
        run: node worker.mjs
"""
new = """      # The canary runs ITS OWN vendored worker, not this checkout's — that is
      # the copy a member would run, and testing anything else would be testing
      # a code path no consumer ever executes. The worker then fetches THIS ref
      # and converges the canary against it.
      #
      # The worker is `update`'s since #768 Phase 5 retired baselining. Pointing at
      # the old path is what made this gate VACUOUS for weeks: the canary flipped to
      # the update mechanism, its baselining worker correctly stood down, and the
      # step passed in zero seconds having converged nothing. Hence the marker check
      # below — a rehearsal that does not say it converged is not a pass.
      - name: Rehearse
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        env:
          CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF: ${{ inputs.ref || github.ref_name }}
          CLAUDINITE_REPO_ROOT: ${{ github.workspace }}/canary
          CLAUDINITE_REPO: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.repo }}
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        working-directory: canary/.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/update
        run: node worker.mjs | tee "$RUNNER_TEMP/rehearsal.log"

      # A green step is not evidence; the marker is. Without this, every way of
      # exiting 0 without converging — a stand-down, an early return, a worker whose
      # path moved again — reads exactly like a qualified release.
      - name: Assert the rehearsal actually converged
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.skip == 'false'
        run: |
          if ! grep -q 'claudinite-rehearsal: converged' "$RUNNER_TEMP/rehearsal.log"; then
            echo "::error::The rehearsal exited 0 without converging the canary — it printed no"
            echo "::error::'claudinite-rehearsal: converged' line. A pass here would qualify a"
            echo "::error::release nothing rehearsed. Check the worker path in this workflow."
            exit 1
          fi
"""
assert old in s
open(p,'w',encoding='utf8').write(s.replace(old,new,1))
print('workflow updated')

barrier crossing this costs is accepted explicitly in the declaration.

the gate fails without it, so every future way of exiting 0 without
converging — a stand-down, an early return, a moved path — reads as the

5: retire baselining

The last phase of #768. Baselining and the update flows have both existed
since Phase 4 so the fleet could cross over one repo at a time; every member
now declares `maintenance.mechanism: "updates"`, so the older mechanism has
nothing left to serve.

REMOVED. `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/` and its escalation codes; the
`migrations/apply.mjs` and `migrations/registry.mjs` compatibility entry
points (#769) and the empty `migrations/` tree with them.

Those shims existed because a member invoked the applier BY PATH out of a
fresh canon clone, using its own vendored worker — as new as its last
converge, never as new as canon. Deleting them earlier would have failed the
apply step of the very converge that would have delivered the newer worker.
That deadlock is gone with the worker that had it.

THE `agentic:` FIELD IS REJECTED, NOT IGNORED. Nothing reads it: the engine
flow never had an agentic lane (DESIGN §5), and the pack flow's apply stage
decides from the version plan — a fact about what the update did, not a flag
a record carries. An ignored field on a record written in good faith is work
that silently never happens, which is the correctness risk the note existed
to close (#405), so `loadMigrations` fails on one and says where the work
goes now. The last record carrying a note (sheepdog's `fleet-baseline-task`)
is drained — the orphaned workflow it removed is gone from the enforcer.

THE DEFAULT MECHANISM MOVES TO `updates`, by the same rule that once pointed
it at baselining: a default may only point at what is already true. The
retired value still PARSES — a mount predating the flip, or a restored
backup, can still say it, and reading that as anything else would hand the
repo to a mechanism its owner never chose — but the update runner now refuses
such a repo loudly and non-zero instead of standing down, because standing
down quietly leaves a repo unmaintained with a green run to show for it.

The sheepdog fleet lever now forces `update`. A lever naming a task nothing
runs still reports a clean dispatch, and that sweep counts dispatches rather
than outcomes (Sheepdog#172), so the wrong id there would have been invisible.

VOCABULARY. Swept where the word named the LIVE mechanism — instructions,
check remedies, user-facing docs, the scheduler stub's own
`FORCE_TASKS=baselining` example. Deliberately NOT swept in two places: dated
migration records and design docs, which describe a mechanism that really
existed and are history rather than instructions; and the unrelated sense of
"baseline" (the baseline pack, baseline skills, baseline migrations), which
a mechanical rename would have corrupted.

The `fleet-baseline` task keeps its name for now — renaming a pack task is
the fleet-wide update lever's own work, not this The live canary is "the required final step of any core change", and it has
been rehearsing NOTHING since the canary repo flipped to `updates` on
2026-08-12: the workflow drove the canary's vendored BASELINING worker, which
correctly stood down and exited 0 in zero seconds. A green step was the only
evidence anyone checked, so the gate reported a qualification that never
happened. (Engine 2's rehearsal predates the flip and was real.)

Three changes, each closing one way that could recur:

REHEARSAL MODE in the update runner. `CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF` clones that ref
rather than the default branch, runs both flows, reports the terminal, and
restores the working tree — no branch, no commit, no PR, and above all no
stamp, since a stamped branch head would leave the canary off trunk and the
next converge's anti-rewind guard would refuse it.

THE WORKER UNDER TEST IS THE ONE THIS REF SHIPS, not the canary's vendored
copy. The old argument — "the copy a member would run" — breaks on exactly
the case the gate exists for: the worker is itself vendored content, so a
change TO it cannot be rehearsed by a copy that predates it. Worse, driving
the canary's copy here would ignore CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF and run a real cycle
against main, opening a PR on the canary instead of qualifying the ref. The
barrier crossing this costs is accepted explicitly in the declaration.

A MARKER, GREPPED. The worker prints one line when it really converged and
the gate fails without it, so every future way of exiting 0 without
converging — a stand-down, an early return, a moved path — reads as the
failure it is rather than as a fast green. With `defaults.run.shell: bash`,

5: retire baselining

The last phase of #768. Baselining and the update flows have both existed
since Phase 4 so the fleet could cross over one repo at a time; every member
now declares `maintenance.mechanism: "updates"`, so the older mechanism has
nothing left to serve.

REMOVED. `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/` and its escalation codes; the
`migrations/apply.mjs` and `migrations/registry.mjs` compatibility entry
points (#769) and the empty `migrations/` tree with them.

Those shims existed because a member invoked the applier BY PATH out of a
fresh canon clone, using its own vendored worker — as new as its last
converge, never as new as canon. Deleting them earlier would have failed the
apply step of the very converge that would have delivered the newer worker.
That deadlock is gone with the worker that had it.

THE `agentic:` FIELD IS REJECTED, NOT IGNORED. Nothing reads it: the engine
flow never had an agentic lane (DESIGN §5), and the pack flow's apply stage
decides from the version plan — a fact about what the update did, not a flag
a record carries. An ignored field on a record written in good faith is work
that silently never happens, which is the correctness risk the note existed
to close (#405), so `loadMigrations` fails on one and says where the work
goes now. The last record carrying a note (sheepdog's `fleet-baseline-task`)
is drained — the orphaned workflow it removed is gone from the enforcer.

THE DEFAULT MECHANISM MOVES TO `updates`, by the same rule that once pointed
it at baselining: a default may only point at what is already true. The
retired value still PARSES — a mount predating the flip, or a restored
backup, can still say it, and reading that as anything else would hand the
repo to a mechanism its owner never chose — but the update runner now refuses
such a repo loudly and non-zero instead of standing down, because standing
down quietly leaves a repo unmaintained with a green run to show for it.

The sheepdog fleet lever now forces `update`. A lever naming a task nothing
runs still reports a clean dispatch, and that sweep counts dispatches rather
than outcomes (Sheepdog#172), so the wrong id there would have been invisible.

VOCABULARY. Swept where the word named the LIVE mechanism — instructions,
check remedies, user-facing docs, the scheduler stub's own
`FORCE_TASKS=baselining` example. Deliberately NOT swept in two places: dated
migration records and design docs, which describe a mechanism that really
existed and are history rather than instructions; and the unrelated sense of
"baseline" (the baseline pack, baseline skills, baseline migrations), which
a mechanical rename would have corrupted.

The `fleet-baseline` task keeps its name for now — renaming a pack task is
the fleet-wide update lever's own work, not this input.title: Phase 5: retire baselining, and fix the two things the migration exposed
input.body:
Closes the last phase of #768, plus #786 and #787 — the two defects the fleet-wide migration surfaced — and one more found while running the release procedure.

Engine 3, qualified by [canary rehearsal 31654827686](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/31654827686).

## #786 — freshness measured by version

The update flows stamp `engineVersion`/`packVersions` and deliberately never write `ref` or `updated`: a no-op cycle must produce no PR, and a date stamped every night is the churn the versioned scheme removed. But `fleet-freshness` measured liveness by **the age of the stamped ref**, which on a maintained member is frozen by design. With one canary that was a curiosity; with the whole fleet migrated it would have reported every healthy member as drifting the moment canon moved past `631a067`.

The sweep now asks the question the member's own mechanism can answer — `baselining` keeps the date measure, `updates` compares installed versions against what canon publishes. That is exact rather than estimated, so a drift issue names the missing version instead of a number of days, and a version-measured member never consults the ref at all: neither the compare call nor the `ref-not-on-trunk` verdict derived from it, both of which would answer a question that no longer means anything. Canon's side is read from canon over the API (never imported — the enforcer's mount is a different commit, and what canon publishes *now* is the question), cached so the fleet's shared packs cost one read each per sweep.

## #787 — a stranded PR is disposed of, not superseded

The runner logged `leaving it open for the next run to dispose of` and no code anywhere could keep that promise: the quiet-cycle early return fires before anything looks at open PRs, so the only cycle that could dispose of a stranded PR was one with its own work to deliver — and that cycle opened a competing PR instead. Seen live on TLDR #246 and CrosswordChat #177.

Disposal moves out of baselining's worker into the shared landing module and runs **before** the converge; the ordering is the fix. It reports which of three disposals happened, because `merged` means main moved past this job's checkout and converging on that stale tree would re-deliver a diff that just landed.

## Phase 5 — the retirement

Removed `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/`, its escalation codes, and the `migrations/apply.mjs` + `migrations/registry.mjs` compatibility entry points. Those shims existed because a member invoked the applier *by path* out of a fresh canon clone using its own vendored worker; deleting them earlier would have failed the apply step of the very converge that would have delivered the newer worker. That deadlock goes with the worker that had it.

The `agentic:` field is **rejected, not ignored** — an ignored field on a record written in good faith is work that silently never happens, which is the risk the note existed to close (#405). The last record carrying one is drained. The default mechanism moves to `updates` by the same rule that once pointed it at baselining: a default may only point at what is already true. The retired value still parses, but the runner now refuses such a repo loudly and non-zero rather than standing down, because standing down quietly leaves a repo unmaintained with a green run to show for it.

## The canary gate had gone vacuous

Found while running the release procedure, and the most serious thing here. The rehearsal — "the required final step of any core change" — drove the canary's vendored **baselining** worker. The canary flipped to `updates` on 2026-08-12, so that worker correctly stood down and exited 0 **in zero seconds**, and every rehearsal since has qualified releases against a converge that never happened. (Engine 2's predates the flip and was real.)

Fixed three ways: rehearsal mode in the update runner (`CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF` → converge, report, restore; no branch, commit, PR or stamp); the worker under test is the one **this ref ships**, since the worker is itself vendored content and a change to it cannot be rehearsed by a copy that predates it; and a marker line the gate greps for, so every future way of exiting 0 without converging reads as the failure it is rather than as a fast green. With `defaults.run.shell: bash`, since piping into `tee` under GitHub's implicit `bash -e` would have swallowed a non-zero exit too.

## Deliberately not done

- **No pack version bumps.** The pack flow replaces each declared pack's tree wholesale every run, so members get the removals regardless. Bumping `basics` would move a version, which is what triggers the **apply stage** — firing an agent session on every member for a change that needs no member-side adaptation at all. If you want the apply stage exercised, bumping `basics` is the lever.
- **`fleet-baseline` keeps its name.** Its `FORCED_TASK` now points at `update` so the lever works, but renaming a pack task belongs to the fleet-wide update lever you described, not here.
- **Vocabulary swept only where it named the live mechanism.** Dated migration records and design docs describe a mechanism that really existed — that is history, not instructions. The unrelated sense of "baseline" (the baseline pack, baseline skills) is untouched; a mechanical rename would have corrupted it.

## Verification

1523 tests pass, `check_the_world` reports 0 blocking, self-test green. The two blocking findings this raised (a barrier crossing and a missing `pipefail`) were fixed rather than silenced — the barrier crossing carries a reviewed `accept` entry stating why. New tests were each watched failing against the unfixed code.

## Follow-up worth filing

`stamp.ageDays` derives from `claudinite.updated`, which the update flows never write — so the update task's own "converged recently, nothing due" precondition branch is now unreachable and it converges daily even when nothing moved. Harmless (it produces no PR) but the same root cause as #786, and it should key on versions.

Three dormant repos (EdFringeAllocator, gRatio, HelloWorldFlutterApp) hold pre-flip mounts. They are declared onto `updates` but inert until woken, and with baselining gone from canon their own vendored copy is what would converge them — which is exactly what the sheepdog-level "update engine on all repos" is for.

---

lastPrompt: fix 786 and 787, do phase 5. We will later implement a sheepdog-level "update engine on all repos" that will bring them up to date, and allow further (agentic, packs) updates.

content.text:
**PR #791 is open** — https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/791 — with CI running. Here's what landed.

**#786 — freshness by version.** The sweep now branches on the member's own mechanism: `baselining` keeps the date measure, `updates` compares installed `engineVersion`/`packVersions` against what canon publishes. A version-measured member never consults the frozen ref at all, so `ref-not-on-trunk` and the age window can't fire on it. Canon's side is read over the API and cached, so the fleet's shared packs cost one read each per sweep.

**#787 — disposal before the converge.** Lifted out of baselining's worker into the shared landing module and moved *ahead* of the converge; the ordering is the fix, since disposal after it is unreachable on the quiet cycle that should perform it. It reports which of three disposals happened, because `merged` means main moved past the job's checkout and converging on that stale tree would re-deliver a diff that just landed.

**Phase 5.** Baselining, its escalation codes, and the `migrations/` compat shims are gone. The `agentic:` field is now *rejected* rather than ignored — an ignored field is work that silently never happens, which is the risk it existed to close. The default mechanism moves to `updates`; the retired value still parses, but a repo declaring it now fails loudly instead of standing down. Released as **engine 3**.

**One thing I went looking for and found: the canary gate had gone vacuous.** The rehearsal — "the required final step of any core change" — was driving the canary's vendored *baselining* worker. The canary flipped to `updates` on 2026-08-12, so that worker correctly stood down and exited 0 **in zero seconds**, and every rehearsal since qualified releases against a converge that never happened. Engine 2's predates the flip and was real; everything after it was not. I gave the update runner a rehearsal mode, pointed the gate at the worker the ref actually ships (a change *to* the worker can't be rehearsed by a copy that predates it), and added a marker line the gate greps for — so a future vacuous pass fails instead of looking fast and green. Run 31654827686 is the first honest rehearsal in weeks, and it qualifies both this tree and the repaired gate.

**Two things I deliberately didn't do**, both reversible if you'd rather:
- **No pack version bumps.** Packs are re-vendored wholesale every run, so members get the removals anyway — but a version *move* is what triggers the apply stage, which would fire an agent session on all 14 members for a change needing no member-side adaptation. Bumping `basics` is the lever if you want that stage exercised.
- **`fleet-baseline` keeps its name.** Its `FORCED_TASK` now points at `update` so the lever works; renaming the task belongs to the fleet-wide updater you described.

Verified: 1523 tests pass, 0 blocking findings, self-test green. The two blocking findings this raised (a barrier crossing, a missing `pipefail`) I fixed rather than silenced — the barrier crossing carries a reviewed `accept` entry explaining why the gate must name the pack.

Worth knowing for the sheepdog-level updater: `stamp.ageDays` derives from `claudinite.updated`, which the update flows never write, so the update task's "nothing due" precondition branch is now unreachable and it converges daily regardless. Harmless — it produces no PR — but it's the same root cause as #786 and should key on versions. I left it as a note in the PR rather than widening this change further.

**Done, all on `claude/claudinite-issue-768-g2qga2` → [PR #791](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/791):**

- **#786** — freshness measured by version for updates-served repos; the date measure stays for anything still declaring `baselining`.

- **Phase 5** — baselining, its escalation codes, and the `migrations/` compat shims deleted; `agentic:` rejected rather than ignored; default mechanism now `updates`. Released as **engine 3**.

**Two problems I found rather than was told about**, both of which would have stayed invisible:

1. **The canary gate had been vacuous for weeks.** It drove the canary's baselining worker, which stood down in zero seconds the day the canary flipped — so every release since 2026-08-12 was "qualified" by a converge that never happened. It now has a rehearsal mode, drives the worker the ref ships, and greps for a marker line so a future silent pass fails instead of looking green.
2. **The Stop hook caught 16 dangling references** the world sweep doesn't judge — deletions I'd made without sweeping inbound references, exactly what `repo-text-sweeps` warns about. Two weren't renames: the `file-placement` exception for `migrations/` was deleted rather than repointed (an exception outliving what it excepted is a standing permission nobody granted), and the pack-independence fixture moved to `updates/pack-update.mjs`, which is the same kind of canon-internal crossing the rule exists to catch.

**Verification:** 1523 tests pass, 0 blocking in both world and work scope, self-test green, CI green on `b84b08f`, and the release row cites the rehearsal of the exact tree being released with only that row edited after it.

**Two judgment calls I'd flag for you**, both easily reversed:

- **No pack version bumps.** Members get the removals anyway (packs are re-vendored wholesale), but a version *move* triggers the apply stage — an agent session on all 14 members for a change needing no member-side adaptation. Bumping `basics` is the lever if you want that stage exercised for real.
- **`fleet-baseline` keeps its name**; only its `FORCED_TASK` moved to `update`. Renaming it belongs to the sheepdog-level updater you described.

One thing worth carrying into that updater: `stamp.ageDays` derives from `claudinite.updated`, which the update flows never write — so the update task's "nothing due" branch is now unreachable and it converges daily regardless. Harmless today (no PR results), same root cause as #786, and it should key on versions. I left it as a note in the PR rather than widening this change further.

content.text:
You're right on both counts, and the second half is worse than a missing bump. Let me set out what I verified.

**Pack migrations are version-gated.** `migrationApplies` is `want > have` — the record's declared `version` against the member's stamped `packVersions[id]`. And `packUpdate` stamps `p.to`, which is the *manifest* version. So a record declaring `version: 2` in a pack whose manifest stays at `1` applies on every cycle forever and never drains. The invariant is: a record's version must be ≤ its pack's manifest version, and to reach already-current members the manifest must bump. My "no bump" reasoning holds only for changes carrying no record — which Phase 5 happened to be, since mount content is replaced wholesale. It would have silently broken any change that did carry one.

**But `.github/workflows/` is worse than gated — it's unreachable.** Under the update flows nothing converges a member's workflows at all:

- `isPackFile` is `packs/<id>/` only, so the pack flow's wholesale replacement covers the mount and nothing outside it.
- The engine flow calls `convergeWiring(..., { workflows: false })` — deliberately, since its Action token structurally cannot write there.
- The pack flow doesn't call `convergeWiring` at all.

So `convergeSchedulerWorkflow` — which stamps the hashed cron and the declared `required_secrets` into the member's workflow — has not run on any member since they flipped. Baselining did it via the withhold handshake: compute the change, drop `.github/workflows/` from the push, hand those paths to the agent stage over MCP. **That lane is the apply stage, which is the one Phase 2 box still unticked.** So the mechanism that would deliver workflow changes is precisely the mechanism that doesn't exist yet.

Nothing is broken right now: the vendored workflow is generic (`node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/run.mjs`), so members keep scheduling correctly, and the scheduler discovers `update` from the refreshed mount. What's frozen is the file itself — including, thanks to my Phase 5 stub edit, an `overrides` example in the GitHub dispatch UI still reading `FORCE_TASKS=baselining`. A member can't receive the corrected text, and a future cron/permissions/secret change can't reach them either.

There's also a coupling worth naming: `applyStage.needed` is `moved.length > 0` — *any* pack version moving on *any* declared pack. So bumping a pack to make a mechanical regex record apply also fires an agent session on all 14 members. You can't ship a deterministic pack migration without a fleet-wide agent stage, which is backwards.

I've filed these as #792 (workflow convergence lost) and #793 (bump ⇒ apply-stage coupling) rather than bolting them onto the green PR.

The sequencing question is genuinely yours, because it decides what I build next:

**(a)** Implement the apply stage now — it's the missing lane for workflows, it unblocks pack migrations properly, and it's the last Phase 2 box. Biggest piece, and the first run of it would be live across the fleet.
**(b)** Decouple the apply-stage trigger first (records declare whether they need it; mechanical bumps stay agentless), then bump `basics` so migrations work again — smaller, and makes (a) safe to exercise on one member rather than fourteen.
**(c)** Leave both for the sheepdog-level updater, since "update engine on all repos" will need the same withhold lane anyway.

I'd take (b) then (a): the coupling fix is small and it's what makes the apply stage's first live run a controlled one instead of a fleet-wide fan-out at once.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a
change, independent of any one project.

- **Starting any requested change** — begin from the *problem*, not the solution, in any
  repository and not just this one. Reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the
  problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way
  to solve it; a different fix, or none, may serve better.

  `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other`, where `other` covers questions,

- **Replying to an automation dispatch prompt** — it is a comment too: classify it, class `other`,

- **Writing that classification line** — put the class **alone on it** and any explanation on the

- **Acting on a correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then
  rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands,
  but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.

- **Acting on a feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements
  document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it
  fail, then implement until it passes.

- **Acting on a process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. Land it as durable
  rules in the project's local scope, its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs), routed
  through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose).
  Promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the
  interactive session's.

- **Choosing what goes on that ladder** — only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and
  outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place.

- **Vetting a rule before it goes on the ladder** — reject two shapes outright: a check that
  asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time), and a
  rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement — take it to the feature
  path, the requirements document and the test that proves it).

- **Landing a rule anywhere on the ladder** — author the assurance first, the check the future
  world must satisfy, execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green.

- **Landing a rule at the prose rung** (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry) — the
  equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

- **Starting work on either build path** — they share one spine: state the expectation in its
  durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it.

- **Building a mechanism for a behavior** — verify against a real run that it isn't already
  provided.

- **Building release, deploy, versioning or CI plumbing** — look for the shared pack that owns it
  first; copying a mechanic from a sibling repo is the tell that it belongs centrally. If no pack
  owns it, report the gap rather than author a third copy.

- **Taking on a task** — minimize its shelf-life, the time from starting it until everyone can
  forget about it.

- **Finishing a change** — watch it work **now**; never park it on "check tomorrow".

- **Changing scheduled or unattended machinery** — force a run now (the scheduler's `FORCE_TASKS`
  lever, a `workflow_dispatch`, the fleet-wide force sweep) and watch it to a terminal state rather
  than wait for its next natural run.

- **Planning a migration** — prefer the design that converges in one forced pass to the one that
  trickles across nightly cycles, accept legacy input at the door so nothing has to wait for
  stragglers, and drive the stragglers with a standing mechanism rather than a phase someone must
  remember to close.

- **When verifying now is genuinely impossible** (an external release window, an upstream fix in
  flight) — make the follow-up a mechanism that comes to you: a scheduled task, a watched PR, an
  issue something converges. Never a human's memory.

- **Receiving feedback that flags a misunderstanding** — check whether the artifact is already
  correct before expanding it; if it is, say so and push back rather than edit.

- **Writing anything** — size it to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three
  paragraphs.

- **Correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source** — derive the corrected
  version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to
  surface what was actually wrong.

## Harness-tool contracts

Three contracts worth knowing before you spend a call rediscovering them.

- **Searching for a tool with `ToolSearch`** — a search that finds nothing is evidence about your
  query, not about the environment. Search the fully-qualified name (`select:mcp__<server>__<tool>`,
  copied off the deferred-tools listing) and try the tool before telling the owner a step is theirs;
  the bare short name returns "no matching tools", which reads exactly like absence.

- **Calling `Edit`** — the file must have been read *with the read tool*; `cat`/`grep`/`sed` don't
  count. The moment shell output tells you which file you're about to change, read that exact path;
  a narrow offset window satisfies it.

- **Needing exact text from the web** — a summarizing fetch tool is not a source; when the bytes
  matter, `curl` into the scratchpad and read from disk. On a `403` don't retry and don't try a
  sibling URL — attribute the search snippet to the publisher instead of asserting it, and mark it
  for re-verification.

- **Seeing a build, test or CI warning** — fix it rather than tolerate it, with a small, targeted
  fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change.

- **Suppressing a warning** — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`,
  swallowing it — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path. Reach for it only as a
  deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected.

- **Keeping a suppression** — **carry its reason at the site**, on the suppression line or in the
  comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected; that inline reason *is* the review
  record, so record no second justification elsewhere.

- **Waiving a finding on *text* rather than code** — try deleting the flagged phrase first; a
  waiver is for a crossing that genuinely must exist.

- **Hitting a sandbox or proxy that denies a fetch** — treat it as a **policy boundary, not an
  obstacle to route around**: don't reach for an open-network runner, an ad-hoc CI workflow or a
  push-triggered "probe", to make the request from somewhere the policy doesn't apply. Answer from
  committed reference material or ask the owner, and say plainly that anything unverifiable is
  unverified.

- **Working around a finding from a vendored check** — confirm the vendored copy is current first;
  the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in.

- **Deferring a warning you can't fix now with a small cause-addressing change** (it waits on an
  upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor) — open a dedicated issue unless one is
  already open, then move on. Resolving it, by real fix or a consciously-chosen suppression, happens
  in that issue's own change.

- **Acting on an approval to merge, ship or proceed** — it applies only *backward*, to the work
  already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A
  later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval.

- **Treating a multiple-choice answer as authorization** — it isn't, even when an option's wording
  mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The
rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`,
   `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

- **Handing over a step only a human can perform** (flipping a repository or console setting,
  granting a permission, adding a secret) — give it **its own issue**, never a note in the PR
  body. The exception is a step whose home is an artifact the human is already editing.

- **Writing that hand-over issue** — give it a checkbox per step, what breaks while each is off,
  and its closing condition.

- **Before handing a step over at all** — confirm you genuinely can't do it yourself.

# Engineering practices

General software-engineering practices, independent of any one project — portable, shared rules;
project-specific rules (architecture, test mechanics) live in the consuming repo's own docs. The
portable git/GitHub-operational practices — branch/commit history, merging, automated-job branches
— live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md); the
mechanics of searching and rewriting text across files — grep/sed sweeps, renames, broken
references — live in [the repo-text-sweeps skill](skills/repo-text-sweeps/SKILL.md); the practices
for writing trustworthy tests — see-it-fail, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser
tests, coverage gating — live in [the writing-tests skill](skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md); and how
to investigate a bug and pin down its root cause — version-gap triage, re-deriving after a failed
fix, probing for a real datapoint — lives in
[the bug-investigation skill](skills/bug-investigation/SKILL.md).

- **Naming a file, module, or symbol** — name it for its scope or responsibility, not the
  technology or mechanism behind it.

- **Referring to a value from more than one place** — prefer a shared constant or a reference over
  copying it, and generate derived data rather than hand-maintaining it. If you can't, add a drift
  guard: the generic `sharedConstants` check for a plain value, or one that runs the real logic
  against the copy in both directions when the duplicate mirrors matcher or predicate logic. Keep
  the guarded literal itself unbroken, since a value split across a line break is invisible to the
  guard and to a `grep`/`sed` rename alike. Have the guard's own text name the places it watches and
  why the split is forced, and don't also comment the duplication — the guard covers it.

- **Writing file A so it depends on file B** — say what A needs from B, or that it delegates, and
  don't re-spell how B does its job. If you're about to paraphrase B's procedure, point at B
  instead. This holds for code comments and Markdown alike.

- **Committing** — one concern per commit: if two changes could each stand alone, split them, and
  a message that wants numbered items is the split talking. Once a commit has landed, revise with a
  new commit, never a rewrite of that one.

- **Working with a file a test or tool generates** — put `GENERATED` in its name, and don't
  hand-edit it; change the generator. Never resolve its merge conflict by hand: clear the markers
  with either side, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit that output. Consider
  automating the clear with a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry, and `git rerere` for a conflict
  that recurs.

- **Writing code that depends on how a platform or runtime behaves** — verify that behaviour
  against authoritative docs or a real run, not a comment or a prior commit's claim.

- **Optimising** — if the change is meant to preserve behaviour, prove it: hash the full outputs
  of both paths across every branch, fuzzing the inputs that select each, and accept only a
  bit-identical match. If the correctness risk outweighs the speed-up, leave the path alone and
  record that as a deliberate call.

- **Needing a library for a narrow job** — prefer a built-in, or a few lines. When the assumption
  that justified an existing dependency lapses, drop it.

- **Answering an edge case a review raised** — first check whether the existing composed rules
  already produce the right answer. If they do, add no production code: pin it with a regression
  test that asserts the contrast case too, plus an accept criterion where you track those, and don't
  re-state it in a comment.

- **Documenting a procedure** — read the authoritative external docs first and write only what
  they don't carry: our failure modes, gotchas, the exact path we ran. Don't document or recommend a
  path you haven't run, however standard it looks.

- **Writing code that can silently do nothing** — a swallowed error, a best-effort fallback, a
  probe-gated optimisation, a hint the runtime may ignore — record which path actually ran,
  reading the state back where the platform exposes it. During development, before the solution is
  proven right, add that debugging information first and remove it later. Without the record, a run
  where the capability never engaged is indistinguishable from one where it did and didn't help.

- **Persisting anything on a user's machine** — put it under the one user-deletable location, and
  extend that location rather than earn a second one. If the platform forces something outside it, a
  registration the OS owns, name that explicitly as the exception.

- **Changing what the software does with a user's data** — the permission string, privacy policy
  and store listing are part of the contract, so change them in the same commit. Retaining something
  new, opening a listener or adding an outbound connection changes the promise rather than adding a
  field: decide it explicitly and rewrite the disclosure before the code. Expect the claim in more
  than one place — grep the whole surface for the standing absolutes it touches ("no tracking",
  "no cookies", "no external assets") and reconcile every hit.

- **Driving an external runtime more than once in a session** — a headless browser, a device, a
  REPL, a deploy target — write one parameterised driver into the scratchpad, taking the target,
  the selector and the output path from argv, and re-point it rather than author a throwaway per
  invocation.

- **Automating something that needs live conversation context** — hook it to an existing human
  workflow event rather than background infrastructure; shell hooks have no conversation access and
  fire per turn, not at session end. Consider changing an existing command's definition — usually
  the cheapest trigger.

- **Writing the exit path of a pipeline or CI step** — an expected, handled outcome exits clean
  with a comment. Reserve non-zero for genuine breakage.

- **Killing a process by pattern** — `pkill -f` matches the invoking shell's own command line too,
  so never chain it, and bracket one character of the pattern (`[h]ttp.server 8099`) to break the
  self-match.

- **Working in a fresh checkout or sandbox** — a setup script may start in the repo's parent
  rather than the checkout, so `cd` in before running anything. A `Cannot find module` there is
  usually an install that hasn't run yet, not a code bug: install and re-run before hunting for a
  code-level cause.

- **Deciding where a config value or a classification lives** — avoid a default; require the value
  explicitly, or make it structural, derived from where the thing lives. Prefer a structural
  classifier to a hand-set field, and collapse a property tracked in several places into one. When
  automation maintains many copies of a config, have it materialize the explicit value into every
  file it maintains instead of interpreting absence.

- **Handling a value that can be unknown** — unknown is a state of its own: never encode it as a
  zero, an empty string or a type's default, and don't let a decoder collapse it into one. Keep it a
  missing key or an explicit null, keep the zero for a real zero, and preserve all three states at
  every stage of a pipeline. Treat absence as a permanent shape of the data rather than a gap to
  close, and where two fields claim the same fact, let each mean what its own source said and leave
  the call to the consumer.

- **Writing a check that scans the repo** — take the file set from `git ls-files` rather than a
  filesystem walk with paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it,
  so a green run isn't coverage of it. When scanning for a forbidden token, strip comments first so
  it matches code, not prose — string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse
  `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs); if the
  scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.

- **Writing a comment** — carry the why, or a cross-file relationship the code can't state itself;
  if the code plus a known convention already says it, write nothing. Describe the current state,
  never the edit that produced it: don't explain the change you just made, and don't note what was
  removed or renamed. If a comment narrates a past fix, keep only the part still true of the code in
  front of you. When it must name a path, spell that path in one canonical place and point every
  other mention there.

# claude-code-web-users-support — for the people working on this from the web

A Claude Code **web** session runs for a signed-in person, in a managed container. A
terminal session does neither. This pack is where the capabilities that depend on that
difference live — anything a project can offer only when the session knows **who** is
here.

## Personal interaction preferences

This project reads each person's **personal interaction preferences** at session start:
how they want to be worked with — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, the
phrases they use to trigger a defined command. If the current user has a file in the
store, its contents are already in this session's context, injected under this pack's
marker by [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs).

**They are not project conventions.** Conventions belong to the packs that own each
subject and load as prose. What this carries is *personal*: the same rules travel with
a person across every project they work in, and two people on one project can want
different things. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project
convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the preference owns only the
trigger phrase.

**The pack holds an address, not the content.** Preferences belong to a group of people
rather than to any one repository, so this project's declaration names the **store** —
a repo, and a path inside it holding one `<email>.md` per person:

```json
{ "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "owner/name", "path": "preferences" } }
```

`path` is optional and defaults to `preferences`. Reading is **local-first**: when this
repo *is* the store, the working copy wins over the default branch, so an edit in
progress is what the session sees.

**Every miss is fail-soft.** No identity (a terminal session has none), no configured
store, no file for this person, a fetch that fails — each is one plain-text note and the
session proceeds on default interaction behavior. Nothing here is load-bearing, and a
nice-to-have must never be able to stop a session from starting.

### If this repo *is* the store

The file name is the **whole address**: the reader builds `<path>/<email>.md` from the
identity the harness supplies, and there is no index, no registry and no fallback. So
every file under `path` is either the store's own `README.md` or one person's
`<identity>.md`; anything else sits in the tree looking fine and is never opened. Two
consequences worth holding: the name must be that person's identity **exactly**, because
it becomes a case-sensitive `raw.githubusercontent.com` path segment that a local
checkout would happily serve either way; and the store is **flat**, because grouping
people into subdirectories makes their files unaddressable.

### Adding or changing a preference

Edit that person's file **in the store repo** — never here, and never in the canon. One
distilled preference per bullet, in the imperative: a preference is a rule the assistant
can act on, not a description of a mood. A preference that turns out to be a project
convention in disguise belongs in the pack that owns its subject instead.

# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.
